Magwitch. The escaped convict introduced in the opening marshes, Magwitch is one of Great Expectations' most transformative figures. Though initially a terrifying figure to young Pip, Magwitch emerges as a profoundly sympathetic character—a man shaped by poverty and injustice into criminality, yet capable of loyalty, sacrifice, and love. His secret identity as Pip's benefactor and Estella's father anchors the novel's meditation on social mobility, guilt, and the redemptive power of affection.

He first appears as a desperate convict pursued by authorities. He terrifies Pip and coerces the boy into stealing food and a file. Yet this act of desperation plants the seed of Magwitch's later devotion. Though he is captured and transported to Australia, his gratitude toward Pip never fades. He becomes a successful sheep farmer in exile through his own industry and determination. Magwitch returns to England incognito to see the boy he befriended, adopting the alias "Mr. Provis" and secretly becomes Pip's benefactor, funding the gentleman's life Pip always dreamed of.

He reveals himself as Estella's father. Her mother, Molly, is the housekeeper employed by Miss Havisham who raised Estella to wound men's hearts. Thus Estella represents the intersection of Magwitch's criminal past and Pip's great expectations. Despite his criminal past and lowly origins, Magwitch's loyalty and paternal love prove purer than the wealth and status Pip covets. His values are moral, not social. He dies after capture, but not before reconciliation with Pip. His redemption comes not through legal pardon but through human affection, completing the novel's meditation on what truly constitutes gentility. Pip is the young man Magwitch rescues and later benefits, creating the novel's central irony of benefaction from an unexpected source. Estella is Magwitch's daughter, whose trajectory parallels his own—both shaped by systems of exploitation. Miss Havisham represents the other figure who shapes Estella, though in a different direction, opposing Magwitch's redemptive influence. Magwitch's arc embodies the possibility of moral recovery regardless of social origin or criminal history, and his story complicates Pip's pursuit of gentility by showing that true nobility lies in character, not class.
